passage: In the summer holidays I stopped having any times at all. I stayed up late watching videos with my brother Lalit, woke up at noon and ate breakfast at lunchtime. By the third week I was grumpy all day and my head felt fuzzy. Then Mummy said school starts on Monday, and my stomach went tight. I didn't want to go back. Mummy didn't shout. She said, "Let's pick two things that stay the same every day." We chose waking up at eight and playing outside after lunch. The first mornings were horrible. But by Sunday I felt more like me, and Monday was only a little scary. My name is Gurleen, and next holidays I'm keeping the two things.

qa.q: What two things did Gurleen and Mummy choose?
qa.a: Waking up at eight and playing outside after lunch.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when Mummy said school starts on Monday?
qa.a: Gurleen felt dread; the stomach went tight and there was no wish to go back.

qa.q: Why did picking two fixed things help?
qa.a: Simple anchors like a wake time and outdoor play brought back a rhythm, so Gurleen felt more normal and Monday was less scary.

qa.q: What might Mummy have noticed about Gurleen during the holidays?
qa.a: Mummy likely saw Gurleen grumpy and fuzzy-headed from late nights, and chose a calm plan over shouting.

grounding: A child's holiday of late nights and no fixed times leaves the child grumpy and dreading school, and simple anchors smooth the return.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, first week after the Puja holidays. Ramesh Dutta.
Arnab came back yawning, pale and short-tempered. On Monday he put his head on the desk during reading and snapped at his partner. When I asked gently, he said, "I slept at two every night. I watched videos. Now I hate mornings and I hate school." He looked close to tears.
I didn't lecture. I asked Arnab to choose one thing that could help this week. He chose lights-off at a fixed time and football at recess instead of sitting inside. I phoned his mother that evening, and she agreed to back him up. By Friday he was joking with his partner again.
Next year I'll send families a note before the holidays: keep one wake time and some outdoor play.

qa.q: What time did Arnab say he slept every night?
qa.a: Arnab slept at two every night.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling on Monday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Arnab felt tired, grumpy and close to tears, saying he hated mornings and school.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do instead of lecturing?
qa.a: Ramesh asked Arnab to choose a helpful change, a fixed lights-off time and football at recess, and phoned home so his mother could back him up.

qa.q: How might Arnab's reading partner have experienced Monday?
qa.a: The partner was snapped at and probably felt confused or hurt, not knowing Arnab was simply exhausted.

grounding: A child's late-night, screen-filled holiday leaves him grumpy and dreading school, and simple anchors like a sleep time and outdoor play ease the return.

passage: By the fifth week of summer holidays in Lisbon, Paulo was going to bed at two after gaming and waking at noon. He was grumpy at lunch and snapped at his mother, Ines, when she asked him anything. And whenever she mentioned school, his stomach tightened. 'I don't want to go back. I'll be so tired.' Ines sat down with him. 'What if we don't change everything? Just two things. Wake up at eight. Go to the park every morning.' Paulo groaned. The first two mornings were hard. By the fourth, he was up before his alarm, keen to get to the football court. On the first day of school, he was tired, but not wrecked, and he didn't dread it as much as he'd thought.

qa.q: What time was Paulo going to bed?
qa.a: At two.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling whenever school was mentioned?
qa.a: He felt dread, with his stomach tightening at the thought of going back tired.

qa.q: Why was Ines's plan of 'just two things' a good idea?
qa.a: It gave simple anchors of wake time and outdoor play without overwhelming him with rules.

qa.q: How might Ines have felt during the grumpy lunches?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and frustrated at being snapped at.

grounding: Shows a child whose holiday routine collapses into late nights and screens, feeling grumpy and dreading school, and how simple anchors ease the return.

passage: At the library holiday club, Aparna, the librarian, noticed Deepika yawning over her book by ten each morning. Normally the most cheerful child in the group, she was now picking fights over chairs and groaning at every activity. After the story session Aparna sat beside her. 'You seem really tired lately.' Deepika shrugged. 'I watch shows till midnight. There's no school, so why not?' Then, quietly: 'But I feel weird all the time. And school starts in ten days. I'm dreading it.' Aparna nodded. 'Holidays can make our days go wobbly. Want to try two anchors? Same wake-up time every day, and badminton in the courtyard with us before reading.' Deepika agreed. A week later she was the first to grab a racket.

qa.q: What time does Deepika watch shows till?
qa.a: Till midnight.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling about school starting?
qa.a: She felt weird and tired, and she was dreading going back.

qa.q: What small steps did Aparna suggest?
qa.a: Waking at the same time every day, and playing badminton in the courtyard before reading.

qa.q: How might the other children have seen Deepika's grumpiness?
qa.a: They may have felt annoyed or confused, since she was usually the most cheerful in the group.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild whose holiday routine of late nights and screens leaves her grumpy and dreading school, and how simple anchors help.

passage:
First week of Diwali holidays: Damini, nine, stayed up past midnight with cousins, watched cartoons till lunch and ate at odd hours. By Friday she was snapping at everyone.
Second week, Sunday: Just thinking about school on Monday week made Damini's tummy flutter. 'I'll never wake up in time,' she told her older sister Shreya, close to tears.
Wednesday: Shreya had an idea. 'Let's both wake at seven from today and cycle round the colony before breakfast.' Damini complained on the first morning, then started beating Shreya to the gate.
The following Monday: Damini woke before her alarm. School felt strange, but she wasn't dragging her feet.

qa.q: When did Shreya suggest they start waking at seven?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: How did Damini feel on the Sunday of the second week?
qa.a: She felt anxious and close to tears, dreading waking up for school.

qa.q: What anchors did Shreya help set?
qa.a: A seven o'clock wake-up and a cycle ride round the colony before breakfast.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt seeing Damini beat her to the gate?
qa.a: Shreya was probably pleased and amused that the plan was working.

grounding: Shows a child whose holiday routine falls apart, leaving her grumpy and dreading school, and how simple anchors of wake time and outdoor play smooth the return.

passage: Damini, sit, let me tell you about my own summer when I was ten. I'm your Vinita Masi, and I was the worst holiday sleeper in our lane. We had one TV and no rules that year. I watched films till midnight, woke at eleven, ate lunch at four. By the second week I was snapping at your mother for breathing too loudly. Then, the night before school, my stomach twisted and I cried that I would never go back. Your Nani didn't scold. The next summer she kept just two things fixed: up by seven, and cricket in the lane every evening. Everything else could float. That June, going back felt ordinary. So, Damini, what time will you wake up tomorrow?

qa.q: What two things did Nani keep fixed the next summer?
qa.a: Waking up by seven, and cricket in the lane every evening.

qa.q: What was young Vinita feeling the night before school, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt dread and fear about going back; her stomach twisted and she cried that she would never return.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Vinita's next holiday go better?
qa.a: Nani chose two simple anchors, a wake-up time and evening cricket, instead of scolding, so the return to school felt ordinary.

qa.q: How might Damini's mother have felt when young Vinita snapped at her that summer?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and annoyed, being snapped at over something as small as breathing loudly.

grounding: Illustrates a child whose holiday of late nights, TV and no fixed times leaves her grumpy and dreading school, and simple anchors smoothing the next return.
